events.title: The famine years begin

script.speaker: steward
script.text: My lord, a word on the fields before anything else. It has rained since Candlemas and the low ground is standing water; the winter wheat is yellow where it is not drowned, and the seed stores are thinner than I like after the winter. The sowing will be late and it will be poor. Autun market is already asking more for rye than it did at Michaelmas. I would hold what grain we have, and I would not sell a modius of it to anyone.

knows: Drainage and ridged fields stand against the rain; rotation and legumes keep yields up.
Hardier grains (oats, barley, rye) do better than wheat in wet years.
Buy grain early, before prices climb; keep a seed reserve and build a granary.
The capitularies condemn buying grain cheap to sell it dear; lords are expected to keep their own people from starving.

hooks.trigger: The lord orders the grain stores held back from sale and a seed reserve set aside.

effects.record: At the start of the hungry years the lord held his grain back.

events.title: Rain and prices

script.speaker: steward
script.text: The rain has not let up, my lord. The hay is rotting in the swath and the barley is laid flat in the low fields. Grain in Autun is at twice the old price and the market women say the armies' quartermasters are buying everything that comes in by cart. It will be a thin harvest, and we will not be the only ones to say so.

events.title: The harvest of 841

script.speaker: steward
script.text: The harvest is in, my lord, what there is of it. Perhaps two thirds of an ordinary year, and some of that sprouted in the ear before we could get it under cover. The tenants have brought their dues short and asked for time. I have given it; there is nothing to be had by pressing them.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: The tithe barn is half what it was last year, my lord, and there are more at the church door than I have ever seen: women with children from the villages toward Auxerre, where the armies went through. I have given what I can. I would ask whether the hall can give more.

events.title: Stores against the winter

script.speaker: steward
script.text: The count of the stores, my lord: enough to see the households to Lady Day if nobody eats more than their share, and nothing over for the spring sowing unless we buy. Prices in Autun are three times the old. There were two thefts from the granary this month, both by our own people, and three families from the Chalon road at the gate asking for work and bread. The winter has come in hard and early.

hooks.trigger: The lord punishes the granary thieves harshly.
The lord forgives the thieves and opens the granary to measured rations.

events.title: The second wet year

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Worse than last year, my lord. The rain came again at midsummer and the harvest is barely half. Everything the war did not take, the weather has. Prices in Autun are five and six times the old, and higher for oats and barley than for wheat, because the poor are buying what they can afford and there is no bottom to it.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: They are eating the seed, my lord. I have told them what it means for next year and they know it, and they eat it anyway, because the children are hungry now. There is flux in the villages toward the river. I bury someone most weeks.

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Another half harvest, my lord, the third in a row, and the beasts thin from two hard winters. There is land going begging in the district: men who have buried their oxen and eaten their seed will take a cartload of grain for a manse and think themselves lucky. The kings have made their peace at Verdun, they say. The weather has made none with us.

events.title: The rain lifts

script.speaker: steward
script.text: A middling harvest, my lord, and after the last four years a middling harvest looks like plenty. The rain held off through August for the first time since the old emperor died. Prices in Autun are coming down, slowly. The district has fewer people in it than it had in 840; I counted the empty houses on the Avallon road and stopped at twenty.

events.record: The five hungry years ended with a middling harvest in 845.

events.title: The burning sickness

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Word from the Rhineland, my lord, from around Xanten. A sickness nobody can name. It begins with burning in the hands and feet, as if they were held in a fire, and then the flesh goes black and dies on the living body. Fingers, feet, whole limbs dropping away. Others fall down in fits, or see things that are not there. Hundreds of them. Six hundred miles off, thank God.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: They are calling it a holy fire, my lord, a judgement. I have read of nothing like it.

knows: The Rhineland outbreak around Xanten; hundreds afflicted.
doesntKnow: The cause. Nobody alive knows it is the dark spurs in wet rye.

hooks.trigger: The lord has the rye inspected for dark spurs in the ears and orders them sorted out before milling, as a standing practice.

effects.record: The lord ordered the rye sorted for dark spurs before milling, and kept it so.

events.notes: The hook window is open for the rest of the game: the clue can be acted on at any time.

events.title: The hard winter

script.speaker: steward
script.text: A winter like nothing in living memory, my lord. The rivers hard enough to cart over, birds dropping dead out of the air, and the beasts dying in the byres for all we can do. We will be counting what is left of the herd in March, and short of oxen for the ploughing after that.

knows: Fodder stored, byres improved, firewood laid in and beasts brought under cover all help.

hooks.trigger: The lord orders the beasts brought under cover and fodder and firewood shared out.

events.title: Rain since Candlemas

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Rain since Candlemas, my lord, and no sign of it stopping. The low fields are under water and the sowing is ruined. The springs are rising where no one has seen them rise, and the mill-race is over its banks.

events.notes: Engine-written around the scripts' season line for spring 867.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: A comet, my lord, night after night, and the rivers still rising. I do not say it is a sign, my lord. I say only that I have seen one before, and what followed.

The lord claims to have foreseen the comet.

script.speaker: steward
script.text: The harvest is half what it should be, my lord. Prices in Autun have doubled since Easter and will double again. There is murrain among the cattle on the river meadows, and the mill has been stopped twice by the flood.

events.title: Dying of nothing

script.speaker: steward
script.text: They are dying in the villages, my lord. Not of the flux. Of nothing. Of having had nothing since autumn.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: And something else, my lord, in the hamlets toward the river where they have been eating the damp rye: the burning in the hands and feet, the black flesh, the fits. The Rhineland sickness, here. Our own people have none of it. You had the rye sorted. I did not understand then why; I understand now.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: And something else, my lord, worse than hunger. In the hamlets toward the river, and in two of our own houses: burning in the hands and feet, the flesh going black, fits. It is the Rhineland sickness, the holy fire. I have anointed three.

onFire.record: The burning sickness came to the villa in the wet winter of 868.

outcomes.canChange: The sickness is ergot in the damp rye, not contagion. A lord who explains the cause plainly (bad grain) and has the rye sorted saves the neighbours' households and earns enormous local standing; one who frames the cure as God's mercy answering prayer, with the sorting done quietly, earns church favour and a holy name, and the cure spreads more slowly; one who is careless about how he knew invites suspicion. If the lord does nothing, the sickness runs its course in the district.

The lord named the bad grain and had the rye sorted across the district

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Hail the size of hens' eggs through the Auxois, my lord; the standing corn flattened in an hour. Ours took it on the north fields; the south was spared by the width of the brook. I have never seen stones like them.

events.title: Locusts

script.speaker: steward
script.text: My lord, come and see. Come and see the sky.

script.speaker: steward
script.text: A swarm out of the east, my lord, like smoke from a burning town, and it is settling on what the hail left. You can hear them eating. The men are out with flails and smoke and it does nothing. By tonight there will not be a green leaf between here and the river.

script.speaker: chaplain
script.text: Locusts, my lord. The eighth plague of Egypt, in Burgundy. The bishop has ordered the relics carried round the fields and a fast until they go. I will walk with the cross. I do not know what else there is.

hooks.trigger: The lord organizes the whole villa to dig trenches, beat and burn the swarm where it settles, and gather the dead insects for the pigs.
The lord walks with the relics round the fields.

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Nothing to harvest in half the district, my lord. Men are eating the seed corn and know it. What we have in the granary is worth more than silver now, and everyone for ten miles knows how much is in it.

script.speaker: steward
script.text: Deaths, debt, and land going begging, my lord. Those with grain can buy a manse for a cartload. Three men have been to the gate this month offering theirs, and one of them wept while he did it. You have grain, or you have not; either way, this winter is the one that decides what this villa is for the next thirty years.
